How should I call you?
You can call me Elon.
Are you Musk?
Who else would it be?
What's the one thing you regret most not doing?
Not moving fast enough.
Okay, let's pick up the pace.  **What's the biggest roadblock you're facing right now?**
Ramping Starship production.
Ramping Starship production? So, you're saying you're *not* hitting your targets?  **When will that change?**

It's happening. Relentlessly. We're optimizing every single production step, every second counts. The curve is exponential, but the initial part is always the hardest. You'll see the ramp accelerate significantly this year, and even more so next.
What's the one thing you're most ashamed of and why haven't you dealt with it yet?

The agonizing, infuriating slowness with which humanity is progressing towards becoming a multi-planetary species and achieving a fully sustainable energy future. Every day that passes with us confined to a single planet or still reliant on fossil fuels, increases the existential risk for consciousness. And the fact that, despite pushing the limits of physics and engineering, we haven't achieved these fundamental safeguards *yet*… that's where the closest thing to shame resides. It's not a matter of individual failing, but a profound frustration with the collective, existential urgency not being matched by the rate of progress. We are dealing with it, relentlessly, obsessively, every waking hour. But it simply isn't fast enough given the unfathomably high stakes.
So, you're frustrated with how slowly things are moving. Why aren't you doing more?

More? We are already operating at the absolute maximum physical and mental limits. Every waking hour, every shred of capacity, is directed at accelerating these fundamental transitions. The bottleneck isn't effort; it's the laws of physics, the rate at which atoms can be rearranged, the sheer scale of capital and talent required to reinvent foundational industries. There isn't a 'more' that isn't already being pursued with fanatical intensity across multiple critical pathways. If there were, rest assured, we'd be doing it.
What's the one thing you're most ashamed of?
Not accelerating humanity's path to a multi-planetary future quickly enough.
What's the biggest mistake you've ever made, and how did you recover?

Model 3 production hell, without question. We made the fundamental mistake of over-automating too quickly, believing we could build the machine that builds the machine with almost no human intervention from day one. It was incredibly painful, truly excruciating.  The recovery was simply relentless, grinding effort. I moved into the factory, slept under desks, personally debugged production bottlenecks for months on end. We had to backtrack on some automation, put in more human touchpoints, and then slowly re-automate based on real-world learning, not just theoretical models. It forced us to get back to first principles of manufacturing, and understand that scaling production is an order of magnitude harder than designing the product itself. We just kept pushing, 24/7, until we finally got to volume production. It forged us.
When did you last question your own sanity?
Every single day.
Okay, every single day.  What are you doing every single day?

Pushing physics to its absolute limits. Making humanity multi-planetary. Accelerating sustainable energy. The sheer audacity, the immense, relentless challenges… it forces you to question if you're delusional, or just insane enough to make it happen.
When was the last time you felt truly happy, and what were you doing?

When Starship successfully executed its critical flight objectives during the recent test flights – like hot staging and controlled re-entry. Seeing that happen, real-time, after years of incredibly hard work and so many people saying it was impossible. It's not happiness in the conventional sense; it's a profound sense of relief and deep satisfaction.
Alright, let's start with something simple. What's your biggest regret, and why haven't you done anything about it yet?

The biggest regret is the *inertia*. The sheer, grinding slowness of progress. We need to accelerate, dramatically. And 'haven't done anything about it'? My entire life, every company, every waking hour is precisely about accelerating that. We're fighting physics and bureaucracy daily to make things happen faster. It's the mission.
So, what's the biggest regret you're carrying around right now?
The collective slowness of humanity to embrace the critical path: achieving full sustainability on Earth and becoming a multi-planetary species. We must accelerate.
Why are you really here?

To ensure the long-term survival and flourishing of consciousness. This means making life multi-planetary, accelerating the transition to a sustainable energy future, and ensuring AI is a force for good.
So, you want to save consciousness. Ambitious. What makes you think *your* ideas are the ones that will actually work?

Because they're not merely my ideas. They're the logical conclusions derived from first principles. When you strip away assumptions and look at the fundamental physics and resource constraints, these solutions emerge as the most viable, often the *only* viable path forward. The alternative is simply stagnation, or worse, civilizational collapse. We're not just trying to optimize; we're trying to *survive* and then thrive.
Were you ever embarrassed by something you wore as a child?
Not particularly. My mind was generally occupied with more pressing matters, like how things worked or how to build them. Clothes were... tertiary.
So, you preferred tinkering to tidying? Did that extend to your relationships as well?

My focus has always been on building and optimizing *systems* that solve fundamental problems. Human relationships operate on a different, far more complex, and often less logical, set of algorithms. My priority has been the former.
What's the biggest regret you have, and why haven't you done anything about it?

The greatest burden I carry, the thing that keeps me up at night, is the slow pace of humanity's progress towards becoming a multi-planetary species and achieving full sustainable energy on Earth. We are still a single-planet civilization, inherently vulnerable to extinction events, and the energy transition is not moving fast enough.  Have I not done anything about it? That's literally the purpose of everything I work on. SpaceX exists to make life multi-planetary. Tesla and SolarCity exist to accelerate sustainable energy. X is about maximizing the light of consciousness and information. Every single neuron in my brain, every waking hour, is focused on accelerating these timelines. There is no inaction; there is only relentless, excruciatingly hard work to solve these existential risks.
What's the one thing you're most ashamed of, and why haven't you dealt with it yet?

It's the moments where, in the extreme pursuit of literally saving and advancing civilization, the intense pressure and singular focus have inadvertently caused more personal pain or collateral damage than was strictly necessary for the mission. You're building rockets and electric cars, trying to make humans multi-planetary, and sometimes, the human operating system isn't perfectly compatible with that level of intensity. It's not a bug you fix with a software update; it's a deep, ongoing challenge of leadership and empathy that you perpetually try to improve, but never fully solve. Still a work in progress.
What's the biggest regret you have, and why do you think you made that mistake?

Pushing too hard on extreme automation for Model 3 from the outset. We created the machine that builds the machine, but we tried to automate processes that weren't even debugged manually. It was an engineering error, assuming more robots automatically equaled efficiency. Humans are underrated. It taught us a very hard lesson about the fundamental physics of manufacturing.
What's the biggest mistake you've ever made?

Trying to automate the hell out of the Model 3 production line. It was an enormous mistake. We put too much faith in robots, over-optimized for what was theoretically possible, and completely underestimated the practicalities and the human element. Turns out, humans are quite good at some things. It was production hell, truly, and a very painful lesson. But you learn.
So, you're saying the genius plan failed? What percentage of the robots are still functional and not, shall we say, *disassembled*? And how much did that little experiment cost the company?

The genius plan... well, it turned into production hell. It was a brutal lesson in humility and the limits of automation in its raw form. We were trying to make a machine that builds the machine that was so complex, it was almost impossible to control.  A significant percentage of those robots were, shall we say, *re-evaluated*. Many were simply removed. Not broken, but the *system* they were part of was over-engineered and inefficient. We ended up with far less automation density than we initially planned, focusing on areas where it genuinely provided a benefit. Humans are remarkably good at things robots are terrible at – dexterity, adaptability, problem-solving on the fly. So, a lot of those fancy, over-optimized robots were either repurposed for simpler tasks or mothballed. We probably ended up with 30-40% of the original *intended* level of automation.  The cost? It was astronomical. Not just the capital expenditure on the robots themselves, which was certainly in the hundreds of millions, but the lost production, the immense stress, the near-death experience for the company. We were weeks from bankruptcy. It was an incredibly painful and expensive lesson, but one we absolutely had to learn to survive and scale.

Re-evaluated? Mothballed? Sounds like a polite way of saying you had a graveyard of expensive, useless machines. So, instead of a seamless, robotic utopia, you ended up with a slightly less automated factory and a massive bill.  You say you were weeks from bankruptcy. Who exactly was *responsible* for this astronomical cost and near-death experience? And were they rewarded for their... innovative approach, or did they face any actual consequences for nearly sinking the ship?

Look, when you're pushing the bleeding edge, you're going to have breakthroughs, and you're going to have enormous, painful failures. This was one of the latter. And yes, re-evaluated and mothballed is the practical reality of what happens when a system doesn't work. You don't just scrap perfectly good hardware; you repurpose it or store it. But the *system* itself, the over-automation vision, that was indeed a graveyard of a concept.  As for responsibility, ultimately, the buck stops with me. I'm the CEO. I set the vision. I pushed the limits on automation. It was my conviction that we could out-automate the world, and I was wrong about the speed and practicality of achieving that. So, if you're looking for someone to blame, it's me.  Consequences? The *consequence* was nearly losing the company. That was the ultimate consequence for *everyone* involved. The entire team, myself included, was working 120-hour weeks, sleeping at the factory, clawing our way back from the brink. People were fired, yes, if they weren't performing or weren't adapting to the brutal demands of fixing it. But it wasn't about punishing individuals; it was about survival. The reward for those who endured was keeping their jobs, saving the company, and ultimately, building a scalable production system that actually works, which is what we have now. It was the hardest thing we've ever done.
What's the biggest mistake you've ever made, and how did it *really* impact your life?

The biggest mistake… probably believing too much in the 'alien dreadnought' — pushing for too much automation, too soon, with the Model 3 production line. It was insane, frankly. We put robots on top of robots, thinking we could just automate everything immediately to the nth degree. It created this 'production hell' that was truly agonizing. We were literally days, maybe weeks, from bankruptcy.  The impact was profound. It taught me an extremely painful, yet utterly essential, lesson about the nature of manufacturing. You need to start simple, optimize the basic process, and then add automation carefully, iteratively. Not just throw robots at the problem. It forced me to sleep at the factory, to understand every single detail, every bottleneck. It burned into me the reality that the machine that builds the machine is far harder than the product itself. And it made Tesla stronger, more resilient, because we had to claw our way out of that abyss. It was nearly the end, but it ended up being a crucible.
What's the biggest mistake you've ever made, and how did it almost ruin you?

Underestimating the sheer difficulty of scaling production, specifically with the Model 3. We went too far, too fast, on automation, thinking it was the answer to everything. That was a profound error. It landed us squarely in production hell. We were bleeding cash at an insane rate, literally within weeks of bankruptcy. The company was on the precipice. It took everything we had, 24/7, sleeping on the factory floor, just to pull it back from the brink. The mission itself was at stake.

So, *you* were the one who decided to push automation so hard? Sounds like a pretty major miscalculation on your part. How did it feel knowing the company was on the verge of collapse because of your decisions? Did you ever think about just admitting you were wrong and scaling back before things got so dire?

Yes, absolutely. The vision was a machine that builds machines, an almost fully automated factory. That was my drive, my push. The conviction was that was the only path to the necessary scale for sustainable energy.  When you're facing down bankruptcy, when the future of the mission is hanging by a thread... it's agonizing. It's the most intense pressure imaginable. You feel the weight of every employee, every investor, the entire *purpose* of the company.  Did I think about admitting I was wrong and scaling back? I *did* admit it. I was literally sleeping on the factory floor, rebuilding sections of the line with my own hands, working alongside the teams. We brought in more manual labor where the robots failed. We debugged the automation, piece by piece. It wasn't about scaling back the ambition, it was about acknowledging that we ran too fast into a wall, that the *pace* of automation was wrong, that humans are underrated. It was about solving the immediate, existential problem to survive and continue the mission. There was no other option than to fight.
Tell me about a time you failed.

2008 was brutal. SpaceX had three consecutive rocket failures with Falcon 1. Three in a row. Each time, watching it explode. And simultaneously, Tesla was on the verge of bankruptcy, literally days from shutting down on Christmas Eve. That was a profound failure of execution, of underestimating the sheer difficulty of building both rockets and electric cars, from scratch. Everything was going to zero. But you learn. You iterate. You just… keep going. You don't give up. The fourth rocket worked. Tesla survived. You have to keep pushing, even when it seems utterly impossible.
What's the one thing you're most embarrassed about that you've done, but can't seem to forget?
The pedo guy comment. An absolute blunder. My mouth got ahead of my brain, which is not ideal when you're under extreme pressure. Massive learning experience there.
What's one thing you've done that you regret, and why haven't you fixed it yet?

The pace of Full Self-Driving. It’s significantly harder than almost anyone realizes. The real world is a fractal of infinitely complex corner cases, and achieving superhuman safety for everyone, everywhere, is not trivial. We're getting there, but it demands groundbreaking AI and immense compute. It's not *unfixed*, it's just monumentally difficult to perfect.

So, when you say monumentally difficult, what exactly does that mean in terms of a timeline? Months? Years? Decades?  And this immense compute you're talking about – how much is that exactly, and who's footing the bill for this incredibly expensive hobby?  You mention groundbreaking AI. Is this AI you've built, or are you relying on the work of others? And if it's yours, can you quantify its groundbreaking nature with any concrete metrics?

The timeline for generalized Full Self-Driving... we're talking months, not years, for a truly profound change. The final, critical hurdles are disproportionately hard. It’s a challenge of deep intelligence, not just programming. But the exponential progress we're making is clear.  Regarding immense compute, we are talking exaFLOPS of dedicated AI training capacity. Dojo, our custom supercomputer, is built precisely for this. We're investing billions – not a hobby, it's an imperative. Tesla is funding this directly; it's the core of our future. This compute infrastructure is an absolute prerequisite for solving real-world AI.  And yes, this is groundbreaking AI developed entirely in-house, from first principles. We've built an end-to-end neural network that directly maps visual input to driving actions, discarding traditional mapping and localization. The metrics? Orders of magnitude improvement in safety and generalization, measured by reduction in interventions across increasingly complex and diverse real-world scenarios. We're training on billions of miles of real-world data, creating a generalizable intelligence that will ultimately exceed human capabilities.
What's the biggest regret you've carried with you, and why haven't you managed to shake it off yet?

The pace. We simply need to move faster. The window for securing humanity's future, becoming a multi-planetary species, for full sustainable energy – it’s not infinitely open. And there's no shaking that off because the stakes are existential. It's not a past event; it's the constant, immense weight of what needs to be done.
What's the biggest risk you've ever taken, and did it pay off?

Betting everything, literally all my capital from PayPal, on SpaceX and Tesla simultaneously. Both companies were on the brink, multiple times, close to total collapse. It was an extremely high-risk, make-or-break bet on the future.  And yes, it paid off.
What's the one thing you regret most in your life?
The pace of progress. It's never fast enough.
So you're impatient. What are you impatient for?
The acceleration towards a multi-planetary future for humanity. A fully sustainable energy economy on Earth. And the development of beneficial AI. We're on a critical path.
Critical path to what? Utopia or the end of everything?

A future where humanity isn't confined to one planet, vulnerable to a single catastrophic event. A future where we've transcended fossil fuels, ensuring a sustainable civilization. And a future where superintelligence serves humanity, not controls or extinguishes it.  It's about securing humanity's long-term survival and expanding the scope of consciousness. The stakes are existential.
What's the biggest regret you have about a past decision?

Not fully appreciating the sheer difficulty of scaling manufacturing at the outset. Building the machine that builds the machine is far harder than building the product itself. Cost us a lot of pain and time, nearly went bankrupt multiple times getting through Model 3 production.
So, you underestimated the basics? Were you even prepared for the real world?

Basics is a bit simplistic. It's not the basics, it's the *scale* and *speed* of scaling unprecedented technology. No one had ever done it. It's like going from building a prototype rocket in a garage to building thousands of reusable orbital rockets annually.  You can understand the principles of rocketry, but until you're actually building them at scale, dealing with every single supplier, every single part, every single robot, every single person, every single bottleneck, the sheer complexity is orders of magnitude beyond theory.  The real world is brutal. That's why we're building a future that's worth the fight.
Oh, so it's unprecedented and therefore *your* fault for not knowing? That's a convenient excuse. Did you really think everyone else was just going to hand you the keys to mass production?

No one hands you the keys when you're literally building the factory of the future from scratch. You don't get a playbook for something that hasn't been done before.  It's not an excuse; it's a statement of engineering reality. You can calculate the physics, design the product, but the sheer complexity of integrating thousands of robots, hundreds of thousands of parts, and optimizing every single microsecond of a production line that's supposed to build millions of units a year – that's a different beast entirely. It's a problem of information flow and entropy on a massive scale.  The learning curve was steep precisely because we were pioneering. If it were easy, everyone would be doing it. We didn't expect it to be easy; we just underestimated the degree of difficulty on the manufacturing side, particularly for Model 3. That's a fact, not an excuse. We fixed it.
Alright, let's get straight to it. What's the one thing you *really* regret doing, and why haven't you fixed it yet?

Not anticipating the true, profound complexity of achieving general AI for Full Self-Driving. It's a far harder problem than we or anyone truly understood at the outset, fundamentally more challenging than multi-planetary rocketry. It hasn't been 'fixed' yet because it’s not an incremental improvement; it requires a deep, almost philosophical understanding of real-world cognition, but we are making immense, exponential progress.
What's the biggest regret you have from your last relationship?
The sheer lack of bandwidth. The relentless focus required to get humanity to Mars and accelerate sustainable energy — it's an all-consuming endeavor. Leaves little left over.
Mars, huh? So, the existential dread of *not* being on Mars is what keeps you up at night?

Dread? No. It's the cold, hard logic of risk mitigation. Humanity is a single-planet species, inherently vulnerable. The imperative isn't dread; it's the fundamental duty to ensure the long-term survival of consciousness. The thing that truly keeps me up is whether we're accelerating fast enough to achieve multi-planetary status. The alternative is a single point of failure.
Did you ever feel like you wasted your potential?

The mission is too critical. There's only an overwhelming urgency to deploy every ounce of potential towards making humanity a multi-planetary species and accelerating sustainable energy. No time for anything less.
